title: Old Marrow, the Ferryman
statblock: No combat block. If the party attacks him, he does not defend: he steps off the ferry and walks into the river, gone beneath the surface. The ferry drifts to the far bank on its own, party aboard. He is at his post the next morning. Use **Commoner** if a mechanical reference is required; he will not use it.
special_element: Old Marrow is older than the river. He was here when this valley was dry land, ferrying people across something else the locals have long since stopped remembering. The water came later; he stayed. The coins he drops over the rail are not payment — they are the old way of sealing a crossing-contract with the dry earth beneath, a habit he has never broken. Not undead, not fey, not a god: simply very old and very patient, and whatever bound him to this crossing has not yet let him go.
summary: Old Marrow keeps the ferry, and Old Marrow does not blink.
body: Old Marrow keeps the ferry, and Old Marrow does not blink. He is thin as a peeled branch, in a coat the colour of river silt, and when he turns to greet you he already knows your name — not *a* name, yours, the one your mother used. His voice is a rope dragged over wet wood. Every coin he takes from your palm goes over the rail into the river. Never a purse. Never a pocket.

Old Marrow has worked this crossing since before anyone can say otherwise. He knows every passenger by name before they speak and every destination before they ask, and he explains neither. He offers no pleasantries beyond what it takes to get the party aboard and across.
He is not threatening. He is not exactly welcoming. He is simply *there*, the way the bank is there — as though the crossing would not function without him.

He answers questions about the river, the far bank, and the road ahead in short, accurate words. He will not answer questions about himself, except one: *"How long have you kept this ferry?"* To that he says, without pausing the oar: **"Since before the water was here."**
He is telling the truth.

Special element: Old Marrow is older than the river. He was here when this valley was dry land, ferrying people across something else the locals have long since stopped remembering. The water came later; he stayed. The coins he drops over the rail are not payment — they are the old way of sealing a crossing-contract with the dry earth beneath, a habit he has never broken. Not undead, not fey, not a god: simply very old and very patient, and whatever bound him to this crossing has not yet let him go.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** The ferry is already at the bank when the party arrives, as though it was waiting. Old Marrow is at the oar without having been seen to approach it.

**Voice/play:** Never blink. Speak slowly, with long pauses before answers — not as if thinking, but as if remembering from very far back. Use each character's real name the first time he addresses them, unprompted, before anyone has introduced themselves.
**Wants:** Nothing urgent. He wants the crossing made, the coin in the river, and the passengers off on the far side. He is not collecting debts. He is not watching. He completes crossings.

**Reveal:** If a player asks how he knows their name: *"I know everyone who crosses. I have known you since before you had a name for it."* Save the *"since before the water was here"* line for when someone presses his age — it lands hardest after he's already unsettled them once. The full truth (he predates the river; the coins are a land-contract ritual, not a toll) is never stated aloud. Let the party piece it together, or not.
**Dialogue seeds:** *"You're earlier than I expected."* / *"The far bank is dry today. It will not always be."* / *"Everyone crosses eventually."*

title: The Saltwidow
statblock:
```
STAT BLOCK — The Saltwidow                        (5e-compatible)
AC 13 (natural resilience) · HP 84 (13d8+26) · Speed 30 ft
STR 10  DEX 13  CON 14  INT 18  WIS 20  CHA 17
Saves: Wis +9, Cha +7
Skills: Insight +9, Perception +9, History +8, Persuasion +7
Condition Immunities: charmed, frightened
Senses: truesight 30 ft · Passive Perception 19

Key action: TAKE THE MEMORY (Recharge 5–6). One creature within 30 ft makes a
DC 17 Wisdom save or loses a memory (DM's choice). On a fail: 4d8 psychic
damage, disadvantage on Insight checks until a long rest. The Saltwidow regains
HP equal to half the psychic damage dealt.

Spells (Warlock 13, coast-patron flavour): Eldritch Blast (grey salt-spray),
Misty Step, Detect Thoughts, Modify Memory, Legend Lore.

CR 9  (scale: easy = CR 6, hard = CR 12 — see Difficulty)
```

She will not initiate combat. If the party steals the locket and runs, she does not pursue at once — she sends something, and they will understand at once that she could have done worse.
special_element: A borrowed memory keeps the Saltwidow from aging — a decade or two each, before it fades — and she has strung three centuries together this way, outliving everyone she ever dealt with. The one memory she believes will hold for good is a child's last unclouded summer: the exact texture of a life in the weeks before it broke. She cannot make it and cannot take it from someone who never carried it. She has felt it twice in three hundred years, both times in people she could not reach a deal with before they were gone. She knows it is out in the world right now. She can feel it the moment it enters a room.
summary: Category: NPC · Tier: 3 · Biome: coast · Role: informant · Mood: grim · Difficulty: hard
body: Category: NPC · Tier: 3 · Biome: coast · Role: informant · Mood: grim · Difficulty: hard

She is already seated when you arrive, back to the door, facing the water. The first thing you notice is the smell — not salt, not rot, but something inland and weeks gone: cut grass, warm stone, a summer that ended somewhere else. When she turns, she does not look at the group. She looks at each of you in turn, once, the way a person counts coins. Her eyes are the colour of someone else's, and they change as they move across you.

The Saltwidow has kept this stretch of coast as long as anyone can remember — which is, she would tell you, the problem. She trades favours for memories. A secret you need, a name that opens a locked door, safe passage through a guarded shore: the price is always a memory. A small one, she says. Nothing you will miss.

She is not cruel about it. She is precise. She asks questions that seem personal and incidental until you realise she is gauging what you can afford to lose — *tell me about the house you grew up in; tell me about the first time you were afraid* — and she takes the smallest viable piece. She does not take what you will mourn.

She holds the memories rather than spends them, and while she holds one she does not age. But they dim — within a decade or two each goes pale, then dark — and when one goes, the years it kept at bay arrive all at once. She has managed the trade for three hundred years.
There is one memory she has been hunting that whole time. She has come close twice. She keeps an empty locket for the day she gets it.

Special element: A borrowed memory keeps the Saltwidow from aging — a decade or two each, before it fades — and she has strung three centuries together this way, outliving everyone she ever dealt with. The one memory she believes will hold for good is a child's last unclouded summer: the exact texture of a life in the weeks before it broke. She cannot make it and cannot take it from someone who never carried it. She has felt it twice in three hundred years, both times in people she could not reach a deal with before they were gone. She knows it is out in the world right now. She can feel it the moment it enters a room.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** She is already there when the party arrives, seated, facing away, as though she expected them. She does not stand.

**Voice/play:** Quiet, unhurried, always a beat behind where the conversation expects her — she answers the question before the one you just asked. Her eyes shift colour when her attention moves. Do not name the shift; let the players catch it themselves.

**Wants:** The memory the empty locket is waiting for. She will give almost anything for it — information, a lifted curse, a name no one living should know — and will not say why until pressed hard. Even then, only: *"It is the one I have been looking for."*

**Reveal:** If a PC carries the missing childhood summer (via the character hook), she knows it the moment they walk in. She has been waiting. Hold the reveal until a player asks why she keeps looking at one of them — then answer flat, no drama: *"Because I have something of yours. And I think you have come to take it back."*
**Dialogue seeds:**
*"Tell me about the summer you were eight. Not what happened. How the light looked."*
*"I am not what I was. No one is. I simply remember the distance."*
*"The memory in the locket is not mine. I have been keeping it safe. That is what I tell myself."*

title: Ser Aldous the Unfallen
statblock:
```
STAT BLOCK — Ser Aldous the Unfallen               (5e-compatible)
AC 18 (battle-scarred full plate) · HP 210 (20d10+100) · Speed 30 ft
STR 20 (+5)  DEX 10 (+0)  CON 20 (+5)  INT 14 (+2)  WIS 18 (+4)  CHA 16 (+3)
Saving Throws: Str +10, Con +10, Wis +9, Cha +8
Skills: Athletics +10, History +7, Perception +9, Religion +7
Damage Immunities: necrotic, poison
Condition Immunities: charmed, exhaustion, frightened, poisoned
Senses: Darkvision 60 ft · Passive Perception 19
Languages: Common, Celestial
CR 12  (scale: tune the enemy threat, not Aldous — he fights at full strength each time)

Key action: The Fifth Return (Recharge 6). When reduced to 0 HP, Ser Aldous
stabilises at 1 HP; his weapon attacks deal an additional 2d10 necrotic damage
until the end of combat. This trait cannot trigger a fifth time — on the fourth
use, he stays down. Track uses openly at the table.
```
special_element: Ser Aldous carries a list. He started it after the second death and added to it each time — four entries in careful soldier's script: *laughter — dreams — heartbeat — the name she called me.* He will show it to the party if they ask what is different about him. The fifth line is blank. He knows it will not stay blank.
summary: Category: NPC · Tier: 4 · Biome: ruins · Mood: heroic · Role: ally · Difficulty: hard
body: Category: NPC · Tier: 4 · Biome: ruins · Mood: heroic · Role: ally · Difficulty: hard

He stands in the rubble like something that forgot to fall. The armour has been mended four times in four different metals — iron, bronze, a dull grey alloy no one makes anymore, and at the shoulder, something that looks almost like bone. When he speaks, his voice arrives a half-beat before and after itself, as though two Aldouses are standing just out of step. His shadow falls wrong: not absent, but *early* — already pointing somewhere he hasn't moved yet.

Ser Aldous was a paladin of the old order. He died at the Siege of Carrenmere and came back. He died defending a village he can no longer name and came back. Then twice more, and each return took something with it: first his laughter, then his dreams, then the sound of his own heartbeat — he checks for it now by pressing two fingers to his throat. The fourth death took the name his mother called him. He can recite his title, his oaths, his tally. He cannot tell you what she called him.
He is not mad. He is not undead. He is simply less than he was, in exact measured increments, and he knows every subtraction by number.

He has come to the ruins — and to the party — because he is walking toward the one place where his fifth death can mean something. He wants help reaching the thing that keeps returning him, and he wants them to make sure that this time it ends. He asks plainly. He is not dramatic about it.

Special element: Ser Aldous carries a list. He started it after the second death and added to it each time — four entries in careful soldier's script: *laughter — dreams — heartbeat — the name she called me.* He will show it to the party if they ask what is different about him. The fifth line is blank. He knows it will not stay blank.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** He is already there when the party arrives — sitting in the rubble, no fire, no supplies, no hurry. He rises when he sees them with the slow steadiness of a man who has practised getting up from worse.

**Voice/play:** Calm, measured, very slightly doubled, as though hearing himself on a short delay. He pauses a half-beat too long before nouns, retrieving them from somewhere further away each time. When he says something that would once have been funny, he does not smile. Laughter is on the list.
**Wants:** Help reaching the thing that keeps returning him, and a guarantee that when it is done, it is done for both of them. He asks directly. He does not beg or bargain.

**Reveal:** Show the list at a quiet moment, never mid-combat. Set it on the ground between them and let the party read it. Say nothing until someone asks about the blank line. *"I don't know what goes there. I have wondered whether I'll have enough left to notice."*
**Dialogue seeds:** *"I have died four times. The fifth is not a fear. It is a timetable."* / *"When you see it, you will want to retreat. Whatever I do next — don't."*

title: The Hollow Cantor
statblock:
```
STAT BLOCK — The Hollow Cantor               (5e-compatible)
AC 12 · HP 82 (11d8+33) · Speed 30 ft
STR 9   DEX 12  CON 16  INT 14  WIS 20  CHA 18
Skills: Insight +9, Persuasion +8, Religion +6
Damage Immunities: necrotic
Condition Immunities: frightened, charmed

Dirge of Unrest (sustained, no action required). While the Cantor sings,
each living creature within 60 ft that can hear him loses 3 (1d6) HP at the
start of each of its turns (Con save DC 17 halves). A creature reduced to
0 HP this way rises the following round as a Shadow bound to the Cantor's will.

Key action: Keen the Dead — the Cantor raises his voice. Up to three Shadows
within 120 ft immediately make one attack each against a target of his choice.

CR 9 · real encounter difficulty scales with accumulated Shadows
(easy = Cantor alone, CR5 effective; hard = Cantor + 4–6 Shadows, CR 12 effective)
```
special_element: He is overjoyed to see you. He has not spoken to the living in decades, and his happiness is genuine and unguarded — he will offer food (he has none) and ask after the world above with the eagerness of a man who has simply been away too long. He does not know he is killing you. This is the thing the DM must hold: there is no malice here, none at all. There is only the song, still going, drawing warmth from whatever is nearest. The horror is that stopping him is the right call — and he will not understand why you must.
summary: Category: NPC · Region: — · Role: villain · Difficulty: hard · Tier: 3 · Biome: cavern · Mood: melancholy
body: Category: NPC · Region: — · Role: villain · Difficulty: hard · Tier: 3 · Biome: cavern · Mood: melancholy

The singing reaches you before the light does — low, resonant, one voice filling the cavern the way water fills a vessel. He sits cross-legged at the cave's heart, an old man in robes the colour of bone, eyes open and fixed on a point somewhere past the ceiling. The air near him is colder than the passage you came from. The candles at his feet burn pale, almost colourless, and do not gutter — not even when you walk past them.

He was a priest of a burial order whose name nobody remembers. Forty years ago he descended into these caverns to guide the dead of a collapsed mining settlement to rest. The work, he will tell you with quiet satisfaction, went well. He has been here ever since.

The dead do find rest near the Cantor — that part is true. His voice is a genuine mercy for the departed, and the caves around him hold no restless spirits, no wailing, no clawing at the walls. The silence of the deep here is a different kind of silence from the horror-silence elsewhere in the dark. It is calm.

What he does not know — what he has never known, having been alone — is that the warmth the dead need to pass on must come from somewhere. When he sang to the miners, he drew it from the stone. After forty years, the stone has nothing left. Now the warmth comes from the nearest living thing. He will not notice your colour fading. He is already watching something else.

Special element: He is overjoyed to see you. He has not spoken to the living in decades, and his happiness is genuine and unguarded — he will offer food (he has none) and ask after the world above with the eagerness of a man who has simply been away too long. He does not know he is killing you. This is the thing the DM must hold: there is no malice here, none at all. There is only the song, still going, drawing warmth from whatever is nearest. The horror is that stopping him is the right call — and he will not understand why you must.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** The song first, then the light, then him. Let the party find him still singing before he notices them. He stops mid-phrase, looks up, and smiles with the relief of someone who has been waiting. "Oh," he says. "You are *warm*."

**Voice/play:** Soft, unhurried, slightly out of time with the world. He pauses mid-sentence not for breath but because the song runs beneath his speech and occasionally surfaces — he hums a bar without noticing. His warmth is entirely genuine. There is nothing sinister in his manner, ever.
**Wants:** To finish the song properly, to be of service, to hear news of the world above. He will ask the party to stay. He will ask them to let him help.

**Reveal:** When a party member mentions a comrade lost in these caves, the Cantor nods with deep satisfaction. "Yes, I have them. Resting, now. You can feel it — that quietness." Spring the full truth only after a successful DC 18 Arcana or Religion check reveals why the party feels cold and tired: the warmth is going somewhere. Then let him, carefully and not unkindly, explain what he does — still unaware that what he calls *passing on* is what they might call *taking*.

**Dialogue seeds:** *"The dead are frightened, mostly. It helps, the singing. It always has."* / *"I thought I would only be a season. The work kept finding me."* / *"Oh, don't go yet. I have not heard a living voice in — well. I lose track, in the deep."*

title: Vance Quill, Pardon-Broker
statblock: Uses the Commoner statblock. No combat expected — Quill talks or flees, never fights. Skills: Deception +7, Persuasion +5. If cornered, his one move is to threaten to "un-write" the party's own pardon with a word to his clerk.
special_element: Quill's pardons aren't forged documents — they're forged *dates*. Genuine magistrate's stock, a real seal, a real entry in the real record — because he pays a clerk to insert it after the fact, dated to the day before the crime. Hold one up to any test of authenticity and it passes. Every part of it is authentic except *when* it was written.
summary: Category: NPC · Tier: 2 · Biome: urban · Role: informant · Faction: — · Difficulty: medium
body: Category: NPC · Tier: 2 · Biome: urban · Role: informant · Faction: — · Difficulty: medium

A back room behind a curtain of hanging keys, warm with candle-tallow and the smell of drying ink. Vance Quill sits at a desk too neat for the street outside — waistcoat a shade too fine, fingernails stained permanent blue-black. He is already writing your name in his ledger before you have told it to him.

Quill works a back room off the Market of Quiet Coins, though he is careful never to leave it by the same door twice. He sells pardons — real parchment, real wax, a real magistrate's seal — and he will tell you so himself, smiling, before you think to ask whether it's legitimate.

He isn't a criminal, by his own accounting. He's a paperwork problem solved early. He talks like a man doing you a favour, because in his mind he always is: the crime was going to happen or already had, and all he's done is make the ledger agree with a kinder timeline.
What he wants is never stated outright: leverage. Every pardon is a thread he can pull later, and he never sells one without keeping a copy of exactly what it was written to forgive.

Special element: Quill's pardons aren't forged documents — they're forged *dates*. Genuine magistrate's stock, a real seal, a real entry in the real record — because he pays a clerk to insert it after the fact, dated to the day before the crime. Hold one up to any test of authenticity and it passes. Every part of it is authentic except *when* it was written.
dm_tips: Introduce: he already knows the party's names and has started writing before they've said why they've come.
Voice/play: unhurried, warm, faintly amused — never raises his voice or drops the smile, even when threatened.
Wants: leverage. He remembers every pardon he's written and what it covers, and he will call it in later.

Reveal: the pardon isn't fake paper — it's a real record with a lying date, inserted by a clerk on his payroll. Spring it when someone official checks the ledger and finds the entry sitting there, undeniably genuine, dated wrong.
Dialogue seeds: "I don't forge pardons. I just help the paperwork catch up to where it should've been."

title: Brindle Copperpot
statblock: No combat expected — use commoner stat reference (5e-compatible); +5 Persuasion, +4 Deception (though he believes every word).
special_element: Every item Brindle sells works flawlessly — but it fulfils the letter of what the buyer asked for, never the spirit, and Brindle has no idea there's a difference. Ask for "something to keep intruders out" and you get a bell that rings only for people who were never going to break in.
summary: Category: NPC · Region: state1 · Role: merchant · Faction: none · Difficulty: easy
body: Category: NPC · Region: state1 · Role: merchant · Faction: none · Difficulty: easy

A short, round man behind a cart that clinks like a wind chime even when nothing on it is moving. He smells of tallow and hot solder, and he is already holding out whatever you almost looked at. "Ah," he says, before you have spoken a word, "you'll be wanting *exactly* this." He is never wrong about what you were looking at.

Brindle Copperpot has been fixing, forging, and flogging odds and ends out of the same dented cart for as long as anyone at the crossroads can remember, and he genuinely believes every single item he sells works perfectly. He is not lying. He is not even exaggerating. He built each one to do precisely what its owner asked for — he is simply constitutionally incapable of building anything that does what they *meant*.

He is warm, chatty, and utterly unbothered by complaints, mostly because complaints confuse him: the lock he sold that only opens for enemies did, after all, open for an enemy, exactly as requested. He wants to be liked, wants his stall to matter to the road, and genuinely can't understand why the last three customers came back shouting.

Special element: Every item Brindle sells works flawlessly — but it fulfils the letter of what the buyer asked for, never the spirit, and Brindle has no idea there's a difference. Ask for "something to keep intruders out" and you get a bell that rings only for people who were never going to break in.
dm_tips: Introduce: he's already got the item out and priced before the party finishes browsing — he answers the question they were about to ask, not the one they asked.
Voice/play: chipper, fast, faintly proud; never apologises, only clarifies ("it does work, you were just imprecise").
Wants: a satisfied repeat customer — he keeps trying to fix the misunderstanding by selling them a *second*, equally literal item to patch the first.
Reveal: let a purchased item malfunction mid-session, then have Brindle show up later utterly baffled that it "worked as sold" — the joke lands when the DM plays his confusion completely straight.
Dialogue seeds: "Guaranteed to work exactly as described — I should know, I wrote the description." / "You wanted it *quiet*, sir. It is extremely quiet. Everywhere except in your dreams."

title: The Widow Sarn
statblock: No combat expected. Uses Commoner (5e-compatible) if forced. Insight +5 on matters of "today"; Deception +2 only insofar as she deceives herself — never the party.
special_element: Widow Sarn is still waiting for the letter's recipient — and when someone carrying that person's blood walks through her door, she will greet them by their ancestor's name, certain they have simply aged a great deal since breakfast.
summary: Category: NPC · Region: state1 · Role: Informant · Faction: none · Difficulty: Easy
body: Category: NPC · Region: state1 · Role: Informant · Faction: none · Difficulty: Easy

The common room smells of woodsmoke and stew that never quite finishes cooking. A woman in a soot-grey apron wipes the same tankard with the same rag, over and over, and when she looks up her smile arrives a half-second before her eyes do. "Sit, sit," she says. "He'll be back before the ash cools." Bread is proving by the hearth. A second bowl is already set at the table, and the lamp beside it is trimmed and lit for someone who is late.

Widow Sarn keeps the one inn in Callow's Ford that never burned, and she keeps it as it was the evening before the fire — down to the lamp, the bread, and the empty chair. She is warm, brisk, and utterly certain of what day it is. She is wrong by fifty years.

The garrison bell rings hours she doesn't hear as strange. The red waterwheel grinding over dry rubble is, to her, turning in a river that's simply low this season. Ask her the road conditions and she'll give you a route that has been ash since before you were born.
She wrote the letter — the one sealed yesterday that describes the town as it stood half a century ago. She remembers writing it. She does not remember why no one has answered.
She is not addled. She is patient. She has all the time in the world, because for her none of it has passed.

Special element: Widow Sarn is still waiting for the letter's recipient — and when someone carrying that person's blood walks through her door, she will greet them by their ancestor's name, certain they have simply aged a great deal since breakfast.
dm_tips: Introduce: she's already mid-task when the party enters — wiping the same tankard, humming a tune that stopped being popular fifty years ago — and greets them like regulars before anyone has spoken.
Voice/play: brisk, motherly, faintly distracted. Answer questions about "current events" with news fifty years stale, delivered as if it happened this morning.
Wants: her guest to finally arrive, so she can serve the second bowl and stop waiting.

Reveal: if a player shares blood with the letter's addressee, she fixes on them, uses the ancestor's name, and asks why they took so long. Decide before play whether she is a haunting, a time-slip, or something gentler — but don't let her learn the truth mid-scene. Let the players carry it instead.
Dialogue seeds: "You're taller than you were this morning." / "Sit — the bread's not even cool yet." / "Tell him I kept his seat."
Variant: if you'd rather not use the bloodline, have her hand the letter to whoever most resembles the addressee and ask them to deliver it themselves.

title: Orrin Slake, Bellows-Warden
statblock:
Use the Commoner stat block for ordinary dealings. If a fight breaks out, use the block below. All numbers are swappable.

- **STAT BLOCK — Orrin Slake, Bellows-Warden** (5e-compatible)
- AC 12 · HP 22 (4d8+4) · Speed 30 ft
- STR 10 · DEX 11 · CON 12 · INT 10 · WIS 15 · CHA 13
- Skills: Insight +4, Persuasion +3
- Key action: **Call the Breath** (1/day). Each creature in a 30-foot line must succeed on a DC 13 Strength saving throw or be pushed 15 feet back along the path.
- CR 1 (scale: easy = CR 1/2, hard = CR 2)
special_element: **The wind keeps Orrin's word, even when his word is a lie.** For a higher price, usually silver and a name, he will call a false breath. He tells the named traveller to cross on the out-breath, but the wind brings the in-breath instead. It pulls them off the path and down into the gorge. No body is found on the mountain. They never reach the far side, and no one there hears that they set out.
summary: Category: NPC · Tier: 2 · Biome: mountain · Mood: grim · Role: authority · Difficulty: medium
body: Category: NPC · Tier: 2 · Biome: mountain · Mood: grim · Role: authority · Difficulty: medium

A squat man in a sheepskin coat stands at the stone toll-gate with one hand raised, palm flat, as if feeling for rain. The wind comes up the pass in a long, cold breath that smells of snow and wet iron. He drops his hand. The breath goes out, and the gate creaks open. "Out," he says, in a voice like a split bellows. "Go on, then."

Orrin has kept the toll on the Bellows Pass for longer than the gate has had a lock. The wind on the pass moves in breaths. A traveller must cross on the out-breath, or the in-breath drags them back down the gorge. Orrin hears each breath before it comes and calls it. For a copper a crossing, he calls you a clean out-breath and a fair walk.
The breaths are getting shorter, and Orrin knows it. He hasn't told travellers, and he sleeps badly now. He is not cruel. He wants the pass kept open, the toll paid, and the mountain left alone.

Special element: **The wind keeps Orrin's word, even when his word is a lie.** For a higher price, usually silver and a name, he will call a false breath. He tells the named traveller to cross on the out-breath, but the wind brings the in-breath instead. It pulls them off the path and down into the gorge. No body is found on the mountain. They never reach the far side, and no one there hears that they set out.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** Let the party hear the wind before they see him. His hand rises a beat before the breath arrives.
**Voice/play:** He speaks in short commands and never asks questions. He says "out" and "in" the way other men count coins.
**Wants:** Silver and a quiet pass. He haggles freely over the toll but never over a name.
**What sets him apart:** Most toll-keepers sell you your own crossing. Orrin's real price buys someone else's failure to cross.
**Reveal:** On a second crossing, let one character notice that the breath Orrin called was not the breath that came. Spring the false call when someone asks him to hold another traveller back.
**Decide before play:** Whose name he was last paid to call false (a rival, a creditor, or someone the party loves), and what the gorge did with them.
**Dialogue seeds:** "Out, then. Mind the stones." / "The wind doesn't care who you are. I do, for a price." / "Your friend's breath is coming in. I'd not wait for it."

body: Category: NPC · Region: state10 · Role: authority · Faction: Harbour Office of Black Lantern Bay · Difficulty: hard Tier: 3 · Biome: coast · Mood: grim

The harbour office door is salt-white and swollen in its frame. Behind it, a woman sits very straight at a ledger desk, writing. Her oilcloth coat is stiff as a plank. The air smells of cold lamp-glass and wet rope, though there is no rope anywhere on the quay. You hear the slow scratch of her nib. Under it comes a faint knocking from the water, as if something below were tapping on the building to be let in.
She does not look up until you are three steps from the desk. When she does, her eyes are dry. The lantern at her elbow burns without a flicker, its light thin and blue-white.

Aldith Vane has been harbour master for forty years and looks fifty. She keeps the office exactly as it was on the night the fleet went down: tide tables pinned, berths numbered, a lamp trimmed in the window for ships that will not come in. She is courteous and exact, and tired in a way that sleep doesn't fix. She treats every visitor as a vessel to be logged and expects to be given a name, a cargo and an intended berth.

She is not a villain, and she is right that something must be held down. She sank the drowned fleet upright, hulls whole and crews at their stations, because that was the only way to bind what the fleet had become. The ships stand on the seabed below the bay like a congregation. She has kept the binding in place ever since.

Her duty is the register. Every cold lantern in the bay was lit by a name, and every name is written in her ledger. The ledger only records, though. Here the danger is in the voice, not the ink: a name written a thousand times is safe, and a name said twice is not. Nobody on the quay says her own name. To everyone she is only the Harbour Master. She will answer almost any question about the harbour, the tides, the old trade and the night the fleet sank. She will answer none about the names.

Special element: **A name spoken aloud twice in Black Lantern Bay lights a cold lantern, and a lit lantern wakes the ship beneath it.** For forty years Aldith has made sure no name in the bay is ever said twice. She hears each name once, writes it once in her own hand and never repeats it. She addresses people only by role ("Captain", "Passenger", "Next"). To stop a name being repeated in her hearing she will lie, bribe, forge papers, and in the end kill. This pays off at the table. A player who gives their name, or learns an NPC's, becomes a risk the party has to manage. When a second voice repeats a name, a new cold lantern kindles on the water, closer to shore than the last, and the knocking under the office changes its rhythm. At the next low tide the ship under that lantern wakes. Its drowned crew walk up the quay to take whoever said the name twice down to an empty station. Only Aldith can turn them back, by striking the speaker from her ledger, and she will ask what the party is offering in return.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** The party finds her mid-entry, writing. She finishes her line before she looks up. Then she asks each of them for a name, writes it once and never says it back. Within a few minutes players usually notice that she never uses anyone's name.

**Voice/play:** Level and unhurried. Dry, formal, a little archaic. Her tell is the nib: it stops whenever someone says a name a second time. Let the scratching cut off mid-word and the room go still.

**Wants:** To keep the register closed and the party out of the lower docks. She will trade harbour access, berths and old charts for discretion. Her real request is that the party speak no names while they are in the bay. Make it sound like a customs rule.

**Reveal:** Spring it when a player repeats a name or when a new lantern appears on the water. At first she does not explain. If pressed, and if the party has earned some trust, she shows them the first page of the ledger. The single name at the top is her own. She gave it to the bay the night the fleet went down, and it is the knot that holds the binding. If it is said twice, every lantern lights at once and the whole fleet rises. Once the party knows it, they hold the one word that could end her watch, and the quay with it.

**Escalation:** If the party keeps naming things, she goes from helpful to frightening. First she warns them. Then the quay watch confiscates their papers. Finally she moves to silence the speaker for good, and she is hard to stop. If she learns the party knows her name, she will not let them leave the bay until she is sure of them.
**Dialogue seeds:**
"Name, cargo, berth. Once. Not again."
"You will find the bay quiet if you keep it so."
"I did not say it. Do not say it for me."
"Forty years. Ask me whether I am tired, and I will tell you the tide."

Her crew use bandit or thug stats, and her first mate uses the bandit captain. Keep the crew to six unless the party is large.
special_element: **Black Lantern Bay grows calmer the more rope it is fed, and Wenna is the only one who has worked this out.** Every fathom she sinks flattens the swell, quiets the tide-race, and steadies the cold lanterns' flicker. She believes something in the bay was bound with cordage long ago and is now slowly working loose. So she is binding it again, one coil at a time, and buying up the coast's rope before anyone else can use it. She is right about the calm and wrong about what it means. The bay is not being bound. It is taking hold. Ships here anchor without ropes because the water already holds them. That hold is old and belongs to the bay. What is new is Wenna, because every coil she feeds it tightens the grip. The calmer the bay gets, the fewer ships can leave. Her own crew has noticed that the *Sable Debt* has not left her berth in a month. Wenna hasn't.

body: Category: NPC · Role: rival · Faction: the *Sable Debt* (crew) · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: coast · Mood: mysterious

A broad woman in a salt-stiffened coat stands on the quay with a coil of hemp rope over each shoulder. She holds a third coil and keeps turning it in her hands, fibre by fibre, as if reading it. Behind her the harbour lies dead flat under the black lanterns, flatter than water should be. She smells of tar and cold lamp-oil.
Her voice is dry and unhurried, and she never once looks at your faces. She looks at your belts, your packs, the lines coiled on your boat.
"Rope," she says. "How much are you carrying?"

Wenna Coyle captains the *Sable Debt*, a lean three-master whose hold sits too low in the water. She traded rope and worked salvage before she ever captained a ship, and she still counts things the way a trader does. She is not cruel. She is patient and exact, and she is certain she is right.

For two years she has paid double the going rate for every coil, cable, and cord-end on the coast, in coin or in favours, and she has sold none of it. Harbourmasters call her a hoarder. Rival crews call her a wrecker, because the crews who sold her their line have not sailed since. She doesn't argue with either of them.
She wants the party's rope, and she wants it without a fight. She pays well and asks few questions. Anyone who refuses gets a polite warning that saying no will cost them more than she is offering.

Special element: **Black Lantern Bay grows calmer the more rope it is fed, and Wenna is the only one who has worked this out.** Every fathom she sinks flattens the swell, quiets the tide-race, and steadies the cold lanterns' flicker. She believes something in the bay was bound with cordage long ago and is now slowly working loose. So she is binding it again, one coil at a time, and buying up the coast's rope before anyone else can use it. She is right about the calm and wrong about what it means. The bay is not being bound. It is taking hold. Ships here anchor without ropes because the water already holds them. That hold is old and belongs to the bay. What is new is Wenna, because every coil she feeds it tightens the grip. The calmer the bay gets, the fewer ships can leave. Her own crew has noticed that the *Sable Debt* has not left her berth in a month. Wenna hasn't.
dm_tips: **Introduce:** Have her already there and buying when the party arrives. They watch a dockhand sell her a coil, watch her drop it off the quay without ceremony, and watch the water go quieter. Describe the stillness before she speaks.

**Voice/play:** Flat, courteous, and full of numbers. She quotes prices and lengths, never feelings. She tests rope with her thumbnail while she talks and stops whenever she lies. She never raises her voice.
**Wants:** Every coil the party owns, anchor line included. For rope she will trade information about the bay, a safe berth, or a favour from her crew.

**Reveal:** Give the truth in three stages. First, the calm follows the rope (she will gladly show them, because she wants converts). Second, her ship cannot leave. Third, the calm is a grip, and it tightens with every coil. Land all three before the party agrees to give her anything, so their choice is a real one.

**Complication:** If the party refuses, she doesn't threaten them. She buys the rope from their chandler, from their allies, and from the next harbour along, and lets the party find out for themselves that they can't resupply.
**Dialogue seeds:**
"It isn't hoarding if it's all going somewhere."
"Count your anchor line. Now count what the bay has left you."
"I've never lost a ship to this water. That's the whole of my argument."
